narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 59.7% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your first-year and third-year class rankings were the strongest influences pushing the model toward predicting failure. Both placed you in the bottom decile of your school, far below the average of roughly sixth decile among students who were accepted. These low rankings signaled to the model that you may struggle with the demands of law school and the bar exam.

Your undergraduate GPA of 3.80 worked in the opposite direction. It is well above the 3.23 average of accepted students and therefore pulled the prediction toward success. However, this positive effect was not large enough to overcome the negative impact of your class rankings.

Your LSAT score of 28, also well below the accepted average of 37, added further concern, though it carried less weight than your school performance. Your family income, gender, race, and full-time status played no role in the decision.

To improve your chances, focus on strengthening your academic record and consider retaking the LSAT to raise your score. These steps would directly address the factors that led to the rejection.
